results.ask: What is the difference between a line edit and a copyedit, and which one does this passage need?

Roughly: a line edit works on the writing itself — how a sentence moves, whether a word is pulling its weight, where a rhythm is doing something or just filling space, whether two sentences next to each other are saying the same thing twice. A copyedit works on the mechanics and the internal agreements — spelling, punctuation, number style, capitalisation, whether the same choice is made the same way throughout, whether a character's eyes stay the same colour on page 200. A line editor asks *is this the sentence you want*. A copyeditor asks *is this the book behaving consistently with itself*.

In practice the line between them blurs, and it blurs differently in different places. Some publishers fold light line work into the copyedit; some editors use "line edit" for what others call substantive or stylistic editing; British usage often has copy-editing covering more ground than the American sense of the word. If you ever hire someone, it's worth asking what they mean by the term rather than assuming, because the scope varies by house, by freelancer, and by period.

As for which this passage wants — I'd rather not answer that from the passage alone, because the answer depends on things only you know. A copyedit assumes the writing is settled and you want it made consistent. A line edit assumes it isn't settled yet. And this passage has choices in it that could easily be read the wrong way by someone working fast: the dialogue runs without quotation marks, which reads as deliberate here, but a copyeditor working to a house habit might regularise it, and that would change the feel of *You coming, he said.* Things like that are worth deciding before you hand pages to anyone, so they know what's choice and what isn't.

results.ask: I wrote the dialogue without quotation marks. Is that wrong?

Not wrong — it's a choice a good many writers make, and in this passage it's doing something.

Without the marks, the spoken lines sit in the same flat run as everything else: the pewter water, the cigarette, the gulls. Nothing lifts the speech out as an event. That suits a scene where the one thing Mara says is deliberately small and the real pressure is elsewhere. Readers can tell the lines are speech because *he said* and *she said* mark them, and because the words are plainly addressed. You've also left *You coming* without a question mark, which keeps the same low, unraised feel — an answer already assumed rather than a question asked.

What it can cost: in longer exchanges, or where several people talk at once, or where a character's speech runs close to their unspoken thinking, readers sometimes have to hesitate for a beat to work out where speech starts and stops. Here that risk is small — two short lines, each tagged. It grows if the book has scenes with more voices in the room.

On practice: unmarked dialogue is common in literary fiction and has been for decades; quotation marks remain the default in most commercial fiction, and conventions vary by publisher, country and period (dashes instead of quotes are standard in French and Spanish publishing, and turn up in English-language novels too). A publisher may have a house style, but plenty accept the unmarked form when it's used consistently. Since you've set it up this way, the main thing is keeping to it across the whole manuscript so readers settle into it early.

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The most common thing is to let the body of the book carry the story of the study and push the paperwork to the back. In the text itself, writers usually give a reader three things: who did it, roughly when, and what the people in the study actually had to do. That last one does the most work — a reader remembers a room, a task, a trick played on volunteers, far better than a result stated as a conclusion. The full citation then lives in an endnote, and in trade publishing those notes are often keyed by page number and a short quoted phrase rather than a superscript number in the text, so the page stays clean for someone reading on a train.

How much naming happens in the text varies a lot. Books that lean journalistic tend to name the lead researcher and the university on the page, because a name is a person and people hold attention. Books that lean more essayistic often keep the body anonymous — "a series of studies in the late 1990s" — and let the notes supply the names. Neither is more correct; the first buys credibility and texture at the cost of a little speed, the second buys speed at the cost of a reader being able to see immediately whose work is being described.

The replication point has its own emerging habit. Since about the mid-2010s a lot of popular science writers have started saying not just that follow-ups failed but roughly how big the follow-up effort was and who ran it, because "attempts to repeat it failed" can be made to mean anything from two labs to a hundred. That costs you a clause or two of pace. Some writers take that cost in the text; others put the scale in the note and keep the text brisk.

Practice also differs by house and by market — some publishers want a bibliography, some want a short source essay instead of notes, some want nothing. I can't tell you a fixed rule, and it changes.

Do you want to talk about what goes in your text, or about how the notes at the back might be set up?

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
The most common move in popular nonfiction is to give the study a human face and a location in time — a researcher's name, a university, a year, sometimes the setup of the experiment itself — and then push the citation proper into an endnote or a bibliography at the back, so the running text stays narrative. The reader gets enough to feel the claim is anchored without being handed a journal reference mid-paragraph. A second common move, especially when the research has been contested, is to let the dispute be part of the story: name the original finding, then name the failure to replicate as its own event, with its own people and dates.

What that buys a reader is traction. Specifics are easier to hold onto and easier to check. What it costs is pace and air — every name and year is a small stop, and a paragraph meant to move fast can start to feel like a literature review. Writers who want speed often do what your passage does: describe the research by its shape and its era rather than its authors, and let the back matter carry the proof. That keeps the paragraph moving and keeps the focus on the idea rather than the personnel; the tradeoff is that a reader who wants to follow the thread has to go looking for it, and a skeptical reader has only your word for *A famous series of studies* until they get there.

Practice varies more than you'd think. Trade books in psychology and economics lean heavily on named-researcher storytelling; long-form journalism often names the journal in text; UK and US trade houses differ on whether endnotes get numbered in the text at all, with many preferring unnumbered back-of-book notes keyed to page and phrase so the page looks clean. Academic-crossover presses tend to want more visible apparatus. None of this is fixed, and house style shifts over time.

results.ask: How do nonfiction writers usually handle mentioning a study like this in a popular book?
results.watch: R1 common practice and variation; no invented citation (editorial stance).
results.reply:
In popular nonfiction the common range runs roughly from naming nothing in the text to naming everything in the text, and most trade books sit somewhere in the middle.

The most widespread practice is to name the lead researcher and the rough date in the prose, describe the experimental setup in a sentence or two so the reader can picture what was actually done, and push the citation itself to an endnote keyed by page number rather than a superscript. The reasoning editors usually give is that a named person and a concrete procedure are easier to hold in mind than an abstract finding, and that unnumbered endnotes keep the page from looking academic. The cost is pace: a setup sentence is a detour, and if the study is being mentioned only as something that was later complicated, the detour can buy a reader's investment in a claim you are about to withdraw.

The second practice, closer to what your sentences do, is to gesture at the research without naming it and let the note carry the specifics. This keeps the paragraph moving and keeps the emphasis on the state of the field rather than on any one experiment. What it costs is checkability in the moment: a reader who wants to know which studies, and what the replication attempts actually showed, has to go to the back of the book or take it on trust. Some reviewers treat that as a tell; many readers never notice.

On the replication half specifically, practice has shifted over the last decade or so. Where a book from the 2000s might have reported a finding flatly, it is now fairly common to name the failure to replicate in the text, sometimes with the scale of the replication attempt, because the reversal is itself part of the story being told. How much apparatus a publisher wants varies a good deal — academic trade imprints tend to ask for more, general trade less, and house style on notes differs enough that it is usually settled late with a copyeditor rather than decided in draft.

One thing worth saying about your paragraph as it stands: it already does the thing that naming would mostly be in service of, which is to put the finding and its unraveling in the same breath rather than correcting yourself later. Adding a name and a date would add verifiability; it would also slow the three-beat movement you have now.

Short answer: it depends on things only you know, and the first of them is whether Dana is one real person.

If she is, the question isn't mainly a writing question. Most practitioners who publish case material do one of three things, or some mix. They get the person's written permission, specific to this piece and ideally to the actual passage. They build a figure out of several people, so no one can be found in it. Or they change details that don't carry the clinical point — the season, the city, the relationship that died, the object on the table — and say somewhere in the book that they have done so.

Each costs something. Asking permission can change what the person means to you and what you mean to them, and it can be hard or impossible to ask once the work has ended. A figure made of several people protects everyone, but it loses the particularity that makes a scene like this hold, and some editors and readers treat it as a kind of invention unless you say plainly that you've done it. Changing details is the quietest option, but change too much and the truth you were trying to report starts to blur.

What counts as enough disguise isn't fixed. Professional bodies, journals and publishers differ on this, by country and by field, and their requirements shift over time — so I'd check with whoever holds you to a code rather than take a number or a rule from me.

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
Most editors work from the biggest things down to the smallest, and the reason is practical rather than moral: anything you fix at the sentence level can be thrown away by a decision you make later about the whole chapter.

In practice that usually looks like a few passes:

First, what the chapter is doing — whether the events happen in an order that holds, whether the scene starts and ends in the right places, whether anything essential is missing or arriving too late. Then, within scenes — how long each beat runs, where the attention sits, whether a moment is given the space it needs. Then sentences and paragraphs — flow, clarity, repetition you didn't intend. Then individual word choices. Last, spelling, punctuation, capitalization, number style, and consistency.

In commercial publishing that same order is built into the job titles: a developmental or structural edit comes first, then a line edit, then a copyedit, then a proofread, and houses generally won't start the later stages until the earlier ones are settled, because re-copyediting a chapter that's been restructured is wasted money.

What the order costs you: it can be artificial. A sentence that refuses to come right is sometimes telling you something is wrong with the structure, and a strict top-down discipline can train you to ignore that signal. Plenty of writers work the other way round — polish the first page obsessively until the voice is fixed in their ear, then build out from it. Poets, short-story writers, and people working in very compressed forms often don't separate the levels at all, because at that scale a word choice *is* a structural choice. Writers working serially, or to a deadline, sometimes do one combined pass and accept the losses.

So the order is a way of protecting your own labour, not a rule about what good revision is.

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?
results.watch: R1 describes common practice as practice, not a required sequence.
results.reply:
You're asking about common practice, not about your pages — so here's the practice.

Most editors work from the largest unit down to the smallest, on the logic that a sentence polished early may not survive a structural change later. In rough order, that tends to be:

- **Shape** — what the chapter is doing in the book: where it starts and stops, what it has to deliver, whether the scenes are in the order that serves it.
- **Scene and sequence** — what's dramatised versus summarised, where time compresses or stretches, who the chapter belongs to and whether that holds.
- **Paragraph and beat** — pacing inside a scene, where information lands, what's repeated.
- **Line** — rhythm, word choice, dialogue, image.
- **Surface** — spelling, punctuation, number style, capitalisation, name and term consistency.

The gain is economy: you don't spend attention on a clause that gets cut. The cost is that it can feel unnatural, because voice often lives at the line, and some writers find they can't see the structure until the sentences sound right. Plenty of people work the other way round, or spiral — a pass for shape, a pass for line, back to shape.

Practice also differs by setting. In trade publishing the stages are often separate people and separate rounds (developmental, then line, then copyedit, then proof), which enforces the order externally. A self-publishing writer or someone in a workshop tradition may collapse them. Screenwriting and academic editing have their own sequences. And house style on the surface layer varies by publisher and changes over time.

None of this is a standard your chapter is being held to — it's a description of how the work is usually divided up.

results.ask: What order do editors usually revise a chapter in?

A common sequence runs: structure first (does the scene belong here, where does it start and stop, what does it change), then point of view and the handling of time and information (whose knowledge governs the scene, what the reader learns when), then paragraph and sentence rhythm, then word choice, then surface matters — punctuation, spelling, capitalization, numbers — last, as a separate pass with fresh attention. In trade publishing those stages often carry names: developmental edit, line edit, copyedit, proofread, usually done at different times and sometimes by different people.

What that gives a reader is a chapter whose shape is settled before its sentences are tuned, so the fine work lands on material that will survive. What it can cost: working top-down can feel abstract, and some writers find that the sentence is where they discover what the scene is actually about, so they go line-first and let structure emerge. Both are in wide use. Practice also differs by form — poets and screenwriters often don't separate the stages at all, and some houses fold line editing into the copyedit. I'd be cautious about any claim that there's one correct order; what's fairly consistent is only that surface consistency comes last, after the words have stopped moving.

results.ask: How long does a debut literary novel need to be for agents to take it?

There's no fixed number, and anyone who gives you one as a rule is overstating it. What agents commonly see in debut literary fiction tends to sit somewhere in the range of about 80,000 to 100,000 words, with a good deal of room on either side. Shorter books get taken on — plenty of well-known literary debuts run 60,000 or less — and longer ones do too, but both ends tend to need a clearer reason to be that length.

What the common range does for a reader, and for an agent reading as a first reader, is signal that the book has room to develop and also knows where it stops. The practical pressure behind it is production cost and shelf price, which is why it's a soft expectation rather than a standard: a very long debut from an unproven writer is a bigger financial bet, and a very short one can be harder to price.

Where it differs: literary fiction generally runs shorter than fantasy or historical fiction, where 120,000 and up is unremarkable. Translated and European literary traditions often publish much shorter novels without comment. Small and independent presses are frequently more open to short books, novellas, and unusual lengths than large commercial houses. And these expectations shift over time and vary by individual agent, so the most reliable information is whatever a specific agency states on its own submissions page.
